content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.88, after using 34 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L3-S1-M3. Then I picked test tasks where the two hypotheses predict opposite results. "Overlap" below means the share of inputs on which a task gives the same response as the closest trained task, from the free `compare` command.

| Test task | New rules | Overlap | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M3, L3-S1-M1 | 0 | 0% | ~11.5 (10 tests) |
| L1-S1-M2 | 1 | 75% | ~11 (5 tests) |
| L1-S1-M4 | 1 | 25% | ~21 (4 tests) |
| L2-S2-M2 | 3 | 56% | ~31 (7 tests) |
| L2-S4-M4 | 3 | 19% | ~36 (6 tests) |

**Evidence:** The deciding comparison is between the first row and L2-S2-M2.
- The first row's tasks reuse only trained rules but share no responses with the trained tasks. They were learned quickly.
- L2-S2-M2 has all-new rules but fairly high overlap. It was learned about as slowly as the all-new control, L2-S4-M4.

Overall, cost went up with the number of new rules, not with how different the task's responses were. The holistic hypothesis predicts the reverse.

**Caveats:** Test results are very noisy; single tests of the same task ranged from 1 to 26. Within the 1-new-rule tasks, the higher-overlap one was easier, which leans slightly toward the holistic hypothesis. I also tested three probe tasks before training, and every task got easier afterwards, so some of the drop may just be general practice. Those three reasons are why my confidence is 0.88 rather than higher.
